575.title: Lift up your heads (Luke 21:5–28)
575.hook: wars and signs; but when these things begin, look up
575.howItsDone: Many churches read Jesus's words about the end in the season of Advent, when Christians prepare both for Christmas and for Christ's return, and they pray in the creeds that he will come again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two coins, more than all. Your line was out of her poverty. What quiet gift did it cost you something to give? Day five hundred seventy-five.

Some people in the temple courts are admiring the building. And it deserved admiring: huge pale stones, gifts hung on the walls, a sanctuary still being finished and enlarged after decades of work. Anyone from a village would stand there with their mouth open. Jesus looks at the same walls and says the days are coming when not one stone will be left upon another. The friends around him want details. When? What sign will tell us? He doesn't give them a date. He gives them something stranger: a long list of frightening things, and then, at the end of it, an instruction about where to point your eyes.

The list is hard to hear. Wars and commotions. Nation against nation. Earthquakes, famines, plagues. Arrests and betrayals, even by family. Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Signs in the sun and moon and stars, and the sea roaring. And yet, threaded through it, are calm sentences. "Be not terrified." "There shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls." Then the turn. "And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh." Notice what he expects them to do. When the news is terrible, the natural thing is to duck, to hunch, to stare at the ground. He tells them to stand up straight and look up. Redemption was a word for buying back a captive or a slave. It's release, coming toward you. Christians read this chapter in more than one way, and churches hold them together. Part of it, many say, came true within a generation: in the year seventy, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Part of it, most Christians say, still waits, for the day Christ returns. Some read nearly all of it as fulfilled; others read nearly all of it as future. Some readers through the centuries have tried to pull dates out of it, but the chapter itself never gives one. What he gives is a posture: when the world shakes, lift your head.
screen: `THE YEAR SEVENTY, AND THE DAY TO COME.`
then, large: `LOOK UP, AND LIFT UP YOUR HEADS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up once today. Right now, settle, and notice your posture. If you've been reading the news or scrolling, your head is probably bent, your shoulders curled in. Breathe out slowly. Now lift your chin a little. Let your shoulders drop back. If you can, look up at the ceiling, or out a window at the sky. Stay there for a few breaths. Think of one thing in the world that frightens you right now, and hold it with your head up instead of down. If you pray, you can bring it to God from there. The bell holds the time.
Lift up your heads. Jesus's instruction for frightening times: not duck and hide, but stand straight and look up, because release is coming.
Your line: your redemption draws near. Today, the next time bad news bends your head down, lift it, and look at the sky for three breaths. Day five hundred seventy-five.

576.title: Watch and pray (Luke 21:29–38)
576.hook: don't let your hearts be weighed down with cares; watch and pray
576.howItsDone: Some Christians keep an evening prayer, such as Compline, to hand over the day before sleep, and some churches read this chapter in the season of Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lift up your heads. Your line was your redemption draws near. When bad news bent your head, did you look up? Day five hundred seventy-six.

Jesus has been in the temple saying hard things about the end: wars, signs, the sky shaking, Jerusalem surrounded by armies. After all that, his closing words are not about armies at all. They're about a fig tree in leaf, and then about something much more ordinary: the weight a person carries all day and takes to bed at night. The unanswered email. The bill. The thing a sister said at dinner. Eleven at night, the day is over, and the mind is still running. His warning reads as if it were written for that hour.

First the tree. When the fig tree and all the trees put out their leaves, you know summer is near. Nobody needs a calendar. You just look. Then a sentence about what lasts: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." And then the warning, in the King James words: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares." Overcharged. The Greek word means weighed down, made heavy. Look at the three things on the list. Surfeiting: the Greek word is used for the heavy head after a night of drinking, something close to a hangover. Drunkenness. And cares of this life. Ordinary worries. He puts worry on the same list as a hangover: both leave the heart too heavy to notice what's coming. Then the cure: "Watch ye therefore, and pray always." The Greek for watch here means to stay awake, to keep from sleep, like a guard on night duty. Not anxious. Alert. Luke ends the chapter with Jesus living it out. By day he teaches in the temple. Every night he goes out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. And early every morning, the people come to the temple to hear him. Watch and pray is not a slogan for a crisis. It's a rhythm: carry the day lightly enough that you can still see the leaves.
screen: then, large: `WATCH YE THEREFORE, AND PRAY ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one care before sleep. You can do a small version now. Settle, and breathe. Notice what's sitting heaviest on you today. Name it, plainly, in a few words. Now imagine it's an actual weight in your hands. You're not solving it. You're just setting it down, for tonight, on the floor beside the bed. It'll still be there in the morning if you need it. If you pray, you can hand it to God by name. Tonight, before you sleep, do it again with whatever is heaviest then. The bell holds the time.
Watch and pray. Jesus's last instruction in his teaching about the end: stay awake, don't let cares weigh your heart down, and keep praying.
Your line: watch and pray. Tonight, before you sleep, name one care out loud and set it down beside the bed until morning. Day five hundred seventy-six.

577.title: The room prepared (Luke 22:1–13)
577.hook: Satan enters Judas; a man with a water jar leads to an upper room
577.howItsDone: Christians remember the upper room on Maundy Thursday, the evening before Good Friday, and some congregations share a simple meal or set a table that night to recall it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a fig tree in leaf and a heart weighed down. Your line was watch and pray. Which care did you set down before sleep? Day five hundred seventy-seven.

Two scenes, running at the same time in the same city. In the first, the city is filling up for Passover, the feast of unleavened bread, and the chief priests and scribes are looking for a way to take Jesus quietly, because they fear the crowds. And one of the twelve slips away to meet them. In the second, two friends are walking through crowded streets with strange directions. Look for a man carrying a jar of water. Follow him home. One scene is a door being opened to darkness. The other is a door being opened to a guest. Luke lays them side by side and lets the contrast speak.
screen: `FOLLOW A MAN WITH A WATER JAR.`

segments.voice: Luke says it in one line, in the King James words: "Then entered Satan into Judas surnamed Iscariot, being of the number of the twelve." Being of the number of the twelve. Luke wants you to feel how close this is. Not an outsider. One of the twelve Jesus had chosen by name. Judas goes to the chief priests and the temple captains, and they are glad, and agree to give him money. Luke doesn't explain why Judas did it. People have guessed ever since: money, disappointment, politics. The text doesn't settle it, and it's honest to say so. Now the other scene. Jesus sends Peter and John to get the Passover ready. Where? He tells them: "there shall a man meet you, bearing a pitcher of water; follow him into the house where he entereth in." Some readers suggest that carrying water was more often women's work, so a man with a jar may have stood out in the crowd, an easy sign to follow. They're to ask the owner of the house where the guest room is. "And he shall shew you a large upper room furnished: there make ready." The owner is never named. His room is simply furnished and ready for whoever the teacher sends. Peter and John find everything just as they were told, and they make ready the Passover. Two doors. One opened for betrayal, quietly, for a price. One opened for a meal, quietly, with no price named. The second, a stranger's spare room, is where Jesus will sit down to the Passover with his friends.
screen: `A MAN WITH A JAR STANDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare a room for a guest. Settle, and breathe. Think of a space you have, even a small one: a spare chair, a corner of a kitchen table, a seat in your car. Picture someone who could use a place to sit this week. A neighbor, a coworker eating alone, a relative you haven't seen. Now picture getting the space ready for them. Clearing the chair. Putting out a glass of water. Turning on the light. You don't have to invite anyone yet. Just let the room be ready in your mind. If you pray, you can ask God to send whoever needs it. The bell holds the time.
The room prepared. A stranger's large upper room, furnished and ready, where Jesus would keep the Passover with his friends.
Your line: make ready. Today, clear one chair, one shelf or one corner and get it ready for someone, even before you know who. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

578.title: With desire I have desired (Luke 22:14–23)
578.hook: he longed to eat this Passover with them, and gives bread and cup
578.tomorrow: I am among you as one who serves
578.howItsDone: Christians keep the Lord's Supper, also called Communion, the Eucharist or the Divine Liturgy, in weekly or even daily worship in some churches and monthly or quarterly in others, repeating Jesus's words over the bread and cup.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger's upper room, furnished and waiting. Your line was make ready. What space did you clear for someone? Day five hundred seventy-eight.

The room is ready. The hour has come. And Luke slows down. Before the bread, before the cup, before any of the words that churches still repeat, Jesus says something personal. A dinner with someone not seen in years, a holiday table after a long time away: there is a kind of wanting that arrives before the food does. Jesus sits down with the twelve, and the first thing he tells them is how much he has wanted this evening.

In the King James words: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." Some readers hear in that doubling, desire desired, a Hebrew way of speaking carried into Greek: very much, with all of me. I have longed and longed. He knows what's coming. And he wants to be at this table anyway. Then something that can surprise a first-time reader: Luke has two cups. First Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it among themselves. Then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to them, saying: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." And after supper, another cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Jewish tradition describes several cups through the Passover meal, though no one can say exactly how the meal ran in Jesus's day. Remembrance, in Greek, is anamnesis. Some Christians hear more than memory in it: the past brought into the present. Here Christians understand the meal in different ways, and it's fair to say each plainly. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans and many Anglicans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Many other Protestants keep the meal as a holy memorial and a sign. Each of them keeps it, because he asked. And then the hard line: the hand of the one who betrays him is on the table. They start asking each other who it could be.
screen: then, large: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share a meal you've longed for. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've been meaning to eat with and haven't. Too busy, too far, too awkward. Picture the table: what you'd cook or order, where they'd sit, the first thing you'd say. Then think about what it would mean to tell them, at the start, before the food, that you've been looking forward to this. Not a speech. Just the truth. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. This week, set the date. The bell holds the time.
With desire I have desired. Jesus's first words at the last supper in Luke: I have longed, with all of me, to eat this Passover with you.
screen: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I have longed for this. Today, before you eat with someone, tell them you're glad to be at the table with them. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 578 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I AM AMONG YOU AS ONE WHO SERVES.`

579.title: I am among you as one who serves (Luke 22:24–38)
579.word: I am among you as one who serves
579.hook: at the table they argue who's greatest, and he tells Peter: I prayed for you
579.howItsDone: Churches that have deacons take the title from the same family of Greek words Jesus uses here for serving, and Christians pray for one another by name, especially for people facing a hard test.

segments.voice: Yesterday, with desire I have desired: the bread, the cup, and a meal Jesus longed for. Your line was I have longed for this. Who did you tell you were glad to be at the table with? Day five hundred seventy-nine.

The room might have gone silent. Jesus has just given them bread and said it's his body. He's just said one of them will betray him. And what happens next, Luke tells us without softening it, is an argument. Over dinner. About which of them is the greatest. It's almost funny, and it's painfully familiar. The meeting where everyone angles for credit. The family dinner where old rankings come back out. The group chat where somebody needs to be right. The friends at this table are doing exactly what people do.

Jesus doesn't shout. He asks a question. Kings like to lord it over people, he says, and then get called benefactors. Not so with you. Then, in the King James words: "For whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth." Everyone knows the answer: the one at the table outranks the one carrying the plates. And Jesus says, I'm the one carrying the plates. The Greek word for serving is the root of the word deacon. Then he turns to Peter, and his voice changes. "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat." Here the King James keeps a detail that modern English can't show. In the Greek, that first you is plural: all of you will be shaken like grain in a sieve. Then the next line goes singular, just to Peter: "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." Peter protests that he's ready to go to prison and to death. Jesus tells him that before the rooster crows today, he will deny three times that he knows him. Hear the order of it. The prayer comes before the failure. Jesus already knows Peter will fall, and he has already prayed, and he's already given him a job for afterward: when you've come back, strengthen the others. The prayer, the fall and the work afterward are all spoken in one breath.
screen: `KINGS LORD IT; NOT SO WITH YOU.`
`I PRAYED FOR YOU, BEFORE YOU FELL.`
then, large: `I HAVE PRAYED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who'll fail. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone heading into something hard: a test, a recovery, a new job, a marriage under strain. Someone who might not make it through cleanly. Picture them. Don't rehearse their mistakes. If you pray, you can do what Jesus did: pray for them now, ahead of time, that their faith won't fail. If you don't pray, hold them in good will, and decide in advance how you'll treat them if they stumble. The bell holds the time.
I am among you as one who serves. Jesus's answer to the argument over greatness: at his table, the greatest one is carrying the plates.
screen: `I AM AMONG YOU AS ONE WHO SERVES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I have prayed for you. Today, before someone stumbles, let them know you're with them, and plan to welcome them back if they do. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

580.title: Sweat like drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
580.hook: on the Mount of Olives an angel strengthens him
580.howItsDone: Christians remember the agony in the garden on Maundy Thursday night, often by keeping watch in prayer for an hour, and Catholics pray it as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who serves, and a prayer for Peter before he fell. Your line was I have prayed for you. Who did you hold up before they stumbled? Day five hundred eighty.

Luke says that after the supper Jesus went out, as he usually did, to the Mount of Olives. As he usually did. This is his place. He's been sleeping out here all week. The disciples follow him in the dark, past the olive trees, and he tells them to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he walks away from them, about a stone's throw, and kneels down. He's close enough to hear and far enough to be alone. If you've ever stepped out of a hospital waiting room to stand in a hallway by yourself, you know the distance. What happens next is the most human Luke ever lets us see him.

He prays, in the King James words: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." The cup, in the Hebrew Bible, can be a picture of suffering poured out. He asks, honestly, not to drink it. And then he hands the answer back. Then two verses only Luke has. "And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him." Notice what the angel doesn't do. It doesn't take the cup away. It doesn't explain anything. It gives him strength to go through. "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were. Luke is making a comparison: sweat falling heavy, like drops of blood. Some readers take it literally, pointing to a rare condition where extreme stress can bring blood into sweat. Others read it as a picture of how heavy the sweat fell. The text allows both. Agony, in Greek, was first a word for a contest, a wrestling match. Here he's wrestling in prayer. One more honest thing: these two verses about the angel and the sweat are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts of Luke, and present in others. Scholars still debate whether they were original, and Christians have read and loved them for many centuries. When he gets up, he finds the disciples asleep, and Luke, gently, gives the reason. They were sleeping for sorrow.
screen: then, large: `AN ANGEL UNTO HIM, STRENGTHENING HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for strength, not escape. Settle, and breathe. Think of one hard thing in front of you that you can't avoid. A conversation, a diagnosis, a long week, a grief. Let yourself say honestly that you wish it would go away. That's allowed; Jesus said it too. Then shift the question. Not, take this from me, but, help me go through it. If you pray, you can ask God for strength for it. If you don't, simply notice where your own strength is, in your breath, your feet, the people near you. The bell holds the time.
Sweat like drops of blood. Luke's picture of Jesus's agony in prayer on the Mount of Olives, when he asked for the cup to pass, and an angel came to strengthen him.
screen: `SWEAT LIKE DROPS OF BLOOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: an angel strengthened him. Today, when the hard thing comes, ask for strength to go through, and notice who or what shows up to give it. Day five hundred eighty.

581.title: He touched his ear (Luke 22:47–53)
581.hook: a disciple strikes a servant with a sword; Jesus heals the man's ear
581.howItsDone: Christians remember the arrest during Holy Week, and some churches, such as the historic peace churches, return to scenes like this one when they teach about nonviolence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sweat like drops of blood, and a prayer for the cup to pass. Your line was an angel strengthened him. What gave you strength to go through something? Day five hundred eighty-one.

Night on the Mount of Olives. Jesus is still speaking when a crowd arrives, and walking in front of them is Judas. He comes close to kiss Jesus. And Jesus asks him, quietly, in the King James words: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" The disciples see what's happening. Someone asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? And before anyone answers, one of them swings. The blade catches the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear. Now there's blood on the ground, swords drawn in the dark, a crowd of armed men, and everything about to get worse.

Then Jesus speaks. The King James has: "Suffer ye thus far." The Greek is just a few words, and translators aren't sure exactly how to put them. Some render it let them have their way. Others say something like, no more of this, or enough. Either way, it's a word to stop. And then a detail only Luke tells. "And he touched his ear, and healed him." Hold that picture. Jesus is being arrested. His friends are panicking. He's about to be taken away to a night of trials and beatings. And in the middle of his own arrest, he heals a man from the side that came to take him. Not one of his own. A servant on the other side, bleeding in the dark. John's Gospel adds two names: the swordsman was Peter, and the servant was Malchus. Luke leaves them unnamed, and the scene works either way. Then Jesus turns to the chief priests and temple captains and elders who came out. You came with swords and clubs, as if I were a robber. I was with you every day in the temple, and you didn't lift a hand. "But this is your hour, and the power of darkness." Christians have gone back to this scene when they argue about violence and faith. Some hear in it a call to refuse force entirely. Others hear a limit on it. Both start from what Jesus did with his hands.
screen: `HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.`
then, large: `AND HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: heal something you broke. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this week, or this year. Is there something you damaged in a moment of heat? A sharp text.
